intro: Günter Kehr conducts the complete Symphony in B minor, Wq 182/5, the fifth of the six string symphonies Bach wrote for Baron van Swieten. Its three movements are marked Allegretto, Larghetto and Presto, and quiet violin phrases alternate with abrupt loud passages.

sections.label: A · Allegretto: exchanges between the violins
sections.mNote: Soft violin phrases alternate with fast passages in the strings.

sections.label: B · Larghetto: short phrases, sudden accents
sections.mNote: Slurred violin figures alternate with sudden loud passages.

sections.label: C · Presto: chords against running strings
sections.mNote: Clipped chords over a running bass; both halves repeated.

cues.title: Opening of the Allegretto
cues.text: The Allegretto opens softly, with the violins playing in imitation over repeated viola notes. The bass rests for two bars before the strings begin their first forte passagework. Short chromatic turns and fast runs pass back and forth between the first and second violins.
cues.evidence: C. P. E. Bach: The Complete Works, III/2, edited by Sarah Adams (2006), Wq 182/5, Allegretto, bars 1–6: quiet violin imitation over repeated viola notes, two bars of bass rests, then forte passagework. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/works/Series%20III/III-2/III-2-Wq182-5.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Van Swieten’s commission, Hamburg, 1773
cues.text: In 1773 Baron Gottfried van Swieten commissioned six string symphonies from Bach in Hamburg. Reichardt later recalled that under this commission Bach could write without regard for the difficulties the musicians would face.
cues.evidence: Sarah Adams, introduction to C. P. E. Bach: The Complete Works, III/2, pp. xi–xii: Hamburg, 1773, and Johann Friedrich Reichardt’s account published in Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung in 1814. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-2-Intro.pdf

cues.title: Larghetto, short slurred phrases
cues.text: The Larghetto is in 3/8. Its short, slurred violin phrases alternate with sudden forte answers, and Bach writes both diminuendo and crescendo into the score.
cues.evidence: Sarah Adams’s edition of Wq 182/5, Larghetto, bars 1–48: 3/8, short slurred figures, contrasting piano and forte markings, then written diminuendo and crescendo. The note describes the movement as a whole. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/works/Series%20III/III-2/III-2-Wq182-5.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trial performance, Hamburg, 1774
cues.text: Before the symphonies went to van Swieten, Johann Friedrich Reichardt led a trial performance in 1774 at the Hamburg home of the mathematics professor Johann Georg Büsch. Bach was present. Forty years later, in an account published in 1814, Reichardt recalled the music’s bold ideas and unexpected turns.
cues.evidence: Sarah Adams, introduction to C. P. E. Bach: The Complete Works, III/2, p. xiv: Reichardt’s account of the 1774 performance at Büsch’s house, published in 1814. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-2-Intro.pdf

cues.title: Presto, binary form with repeats
cues.text: The Presto sets short chords in the violins against running figures in the lower strings. Both of its two large halves are marked to be repeated, so the interruptions and sudden drops in volume come back before the closing bars.
cues.evidence: Sarah Adams’s edition of Wq 182/5, Presto, opening bars and repeat signs; Peter Wollny’s symphonies preface describes the binary finales and their repeats. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/works/Series%20III/III-2/III-2-Wq182-5.pdf ; https://www.cpebach.org/prefaces/symphonies-preface
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Manuscript copies, Hamburg, 1777
cues.text: The six symphonies were not published during Bach’s lifetime. In 1777 the Hamburg dealer Johann Christoph Westphal advertised manuscript copies, and Bach was angry that the works he had written for van Swieten were being offered for sale.
cues.evidence: Sarah Adams, introduction to C. P. E. Bach: The Complete Works, III/2, pp. xiv–xv: Westphal’s 1777 catalogue and his letter of 29 May 1789 recounting Bach’s reaction. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-2-Intro.pdf

fields.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: lawful commercial publication no later than January 1961, before 1963.
fields.note: HiFi/Stereo Review reviewed this exact Vox catalogue and performance in January 1961. Internet Archive dates the issue 1959, corroborated by the sleeve’s 1959 copyright notice, but the rights assessment uses the independently documented 1961 publication bound. Under the project’s eu-published-before-1963 rule, the former 50-year phonogram term expired before the extension applied on 1 November 2013. US recording rights remain unestablished. Internet Archive supplies no Creative Commons licence. Clearance here is territorial, not worldwide.

composer.epithet: Accompanist to Frederick the Great and composer of keyboard music known for abrupt interruptions and trembling single notes.
facts: His father, Johann Sebastian Bach; studied law in Leipzig and Frankfurt an der Oder
Frederick II’s harpsichordist, 1740–67 · Hamburg music director, 1768–88
Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, 1753 and 1762
Wq: Alfred Wotquenne · H: E. Eugene Helm

quote.text: A musician can move others only if he is moved himself.
quote.source: Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, Part I, chapter 3, §13 (1753); our translation

composer.background:
On 12 October 1772, Charles Burney dined with Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach in Hamburg. Bach’s wife, his lawyer son, his daughter and three or four friends were present; upstairs was a music room hung with pictures, drawings and prints of more than a hundred and fifty musicians. Before dinner Bach had played his Silbermann clavichord; after dinner Burney persuaded him to return to the keyboard, and he played until nearly eleven. As he played, his eyes became fixed and his lower lip dropped. Burney wrote that on a long note Bach could draw from the clavichord “a cry of sorrow and complaint”.

Emanuel was born in Weimar on 8 March 1714, the second surviving son of Johann Sebastian Bach and Maria Barbara. Telemann was his godfather. The household moved to Cöthen in 1717 and Leipzig in 1723, when Sebastian became Thomaskantor. Visiting musicians came to play for his father; the boy heard them at home. “In composition and keyboard playing I never had any teacher other than my father,” he wrote in the autobiography published in 1773.
